summary:
Indonesia is a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, so the provision reaches all consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates that prosecutions are selective rather than systematic.

Provincial criminalisation remains in force in two of Indonesia's provinces. The Human Dignity Trust country profile records that Aceh and South Sumatra criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women, alongside national provisions targeting morality. In Aceh, where Sharia law applies, two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025. Punishments there are imposed under provincial religious law and bind anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors.

Enforcement also takes the form of venue raids. On 22 June 2025 Indonesian police raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after public reports of a "gay party" and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman. Amnesty International's Deputy Director Wirya Adiwena described the operation as a blatant violation of human rights and privacy and stated that the gathering violated no law.

A trans traveller has died in Indonesian custody. Rodrigo Ventocilla Ventosilla, a Harvard student and trans activist from Peru, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges while on honeymoon in Bali in 2022. During a WhatsApp call, his mother in Lima was told that authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody; his mother alleges that police beat him, while Indonesian police have denied that violence was used.

Official policy now frames LGBTQ+ people as a security matter. A presidential decree issued by President Prabowo Subianto in October 2025 lists nonmilitary threats and places LGBTQ+ people within national defence policy as risks to be monitored and controlled. Reporting from August 2026 ties that framing to a wave of vigilante attacks on transgender women, with mobs attacking trans people as the government codifies anti-LGBTQ+ attitudes into law. Commentators quoted by ABC News state that the regulation moved hostile rhetoric into the official doctrine of national defence policy.

Banten carries no provincial criminalisation of same-sex relations in the sources examined, unlike Aceh and South Sumatra, and no Banten-specific statute, ordinance, raid, protection mechanism or service is documented in anything reviewed. A visitor in Banten therefore stands under the national framework those sources set out rather than under any provincial religious penalty.

Banten is one of nine provinces where the Ministry of Home Affairs has conducted outreach to issue identity papers to transgender residents since June 2021, the others being West Java, Central Java, East Java, North Sumatra, South Sumatra, South Sulawesi, Lampung and Papua. The stated reason was that many of those people were undocumented, especially where families did not approve of their transition. The programme concerns identity documents for transgender Indonesians; nothing reviewed states whether it extends to foreign visitors or affects passport or entry requirements.
tangentialFactors:
Indonesian provinces diverge sharply on same-sex conduct, which makes provincial location the main variable in expected exposure. Aceh and South Sumatra criminalise it under provincial law, while Banten does not appear among the provinces with such a regime in the sources examined. A visitor's risk profile can therefore differ between one province and the next, but the national penal code reaches every province.

The June 2025 villa raid near Bogor shows that enforcement can be triggered by public reporting about a private gathering rather than by an investigation into identity, and that the scale of arrest can be large. Amnesty International's characterisation of the operation as a violation of privacy and human rights indicates that a raid does not depend on a substantiated legal violation.

The October 2025 presidential decree and the vigilante attacks reported in August 2026 suggest that hostility is being absorbed into official doctrine as well as appearing on the street. That combination raises the chance of third-party violence against trans people in Indonesia and of weak official response, as reflected in the disputed account of Ventocilla Ventosilla's 2022 death in custody.

The Ministry of Home Affairs identity-document outreach gives transgender Indonesians in nine provinces, including Banten, a route into the national identification system. That programme distinguishes Banten from provinces where transgender residents remain undocumented, but it is a resident initiative and no source reviewed connects it to visa, immigration or border requirements for trans visitors.

outOfScopeNotes:
Two of the sources reviewed are not available in full text for this record: a 2022 wire report on police denying mistreatment after the death of a foreign transgender activist in drug-related custody, and an August 2026 feature on repression of Indonesia's transgender community. Only the summary material for those two items has been examined, so their supporting detail remains unresolved.

Whether any Banten provincial or municipal instrument addresses gender identity or same-sex conduct is not established by the sources reviewed. Absence of such a provision in this record reflects what has been documented, not a finding that none exists.

Whether the Ministry of Home Affairs identity-document outreach in Banten has reached a stated proportion of the transgender population, whether it is continuing at its June 2021 level of coverage, and whether the e-KTP obtained under it is accepted across all provincial services remain unresolved in the sources reviewed.

No source reviewed addresses entry, visa or border-screening requirements for trans visitors in Banten, or whether passport markers and physical presentation are examined on arrival in this province.
